solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Incorrect statement about Disney character, about right for tycoon?

indicators.note: something placed about another goes round it, so one piece wraps the next

parts.note: Disney's Pluto is a dog, so calling him a 'Pluto cat' is a false statement about him
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone makes a false remark about a cartoon dog, then asks whether 'about right' describes a business magnate.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'about' belongs inside the phrase: the wrong statement is 'Pluto (is a) cat'. The second 'about' puts that phrase round R, splitting it after PLUTOC.
explanation.definitionFit: A plutocrat is a person whose power comes from great wealth, exactly what a rich business magnate is.

clue.text: What demonstrates strength of spirit

definitions.meaning: first meaning: evidence that establishes something as true
second meaning: the measure of alcohol content in a distilled drink

explanation.walkthrough: 'Strength of spirit' reads like courage or moral fortitude, but spirit here is whisky or gin and its strength is a measured number.
explanation.definitionFit: One word covers both conclusive evidence for a claim and the standard scale for the alcoholic content of liquor.

clue.text: Very young infants have small playgroup, independently

parts.note: babies not yet a year old are 'under-ones'
to have something is to own it
S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a team is a group that plays together

explanation.surface: A note about babies under one getting their own little nursery group to play in separately.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very young infants' is a single unit: nursery and childcare language groups babies under twelve months as 'under-ones'. 'Playgroup' must be read as a group that plays, not a preschool.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something under your own steam is an idiom for managing it alone, without help or outside power.

clue.text: Neat Yankee fellow seen with medical department's hospital equipment

parts.note: neat is an old word for cattle, and an ox is one of them
Yankee is Y in the NATO phonetic alphabet
a gent is a man, a fellow
ENT (ear, nose and throat) is a hospital department, plus the 's

explanation.surface: A tidy American man is spotted alongside the kit belonging to a hospital's medical department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neat' looks like tidy, but it is the archaic word for cattle. ENT is the ear, nose and throat department.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxygen tents are plastic canopies placed over a bed to give a patient air enriched with oxygen, standard ward apparatus.

clue.text: For these jobs the academic not always in the end cut out

indicators.note: taking the end every time means the final letter of each word in turn

parts.words: For these jobs the academic not
parts.note: the closing letters of these six words, in order

explanation.surface: A gloomy remark that, for these posts, the scholar is not always the one who makes the final cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not always' looks like a phrase on its own, but 'not' is the last word of the fodder and 'always in the end' is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: In surgery, to resect is to remove part of an organ or tissue, which is cutting it out.

clue.text: Bash we do with champagne

indicators.note: to bash something is to batter it out of shape, so the letters get knocked about

parts.note: the letters as printed

explanation.surface: A party we will be throwing with champagne to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bash' looks like the party itself, but it is the anagram instruction. The famous champagne house Veuve Clicquot means 'Widow Clicquot', and its fizz is nicknamed after that.
explanation.definitionFit: Veuve Clicquot champagne is affectionately called 'the widow', since veuve is French for widow.

clue.text: Bout follows live match

parts.note: to be is to exist, to live
a bout of coughing is a fit

explanation.surface: A boxing report: the bout comes after a match shown live.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Follows' places the first-named piece after the second, so the wordplay reads backwards from the clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: To befit something is to suit it or be appropriate to it, as clothes match an occasion.

clue.text: Link with firms keeping judge and journalist in work

parts.note: a bridge links two places

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one piece holds another inside

parts.note: as a verb: exercise firms or tones muscles
J is the abbreviation for judge

explanation.surface: A connection with companies that employ both a judge and a journalist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firms' looks like a plural noun for companies but is a verb. 'Work' means a work of fiction: Helen Fielding's diarist becomes a TV journalist.
explanation.definitionFit: Bridget Jones, heroine of Helen Fielding's novels and films, works in publishing and then as a television reporter.

clue.text: Conflict with rank in decline, mostly

indicators.note: one thing set in another sits inside it
mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: a falloff is a decline
rank as in foul-smelling

explanation.surface: A soldier's position slipping produces a clash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rank' looks like a military grade, but it is the adjective for a bad smell. The two-word answer phrase 'fall foul of' is split after FALL, not where the longer piece breaks.
explanation.definitionFit: To fall foul of someone or something is an idiom for coming into conflict or trouble with them.

clue.text: Disapproved of cheers? The opposite!

parts.note: cheers and ta are both British slang for thanks
the opposite of a cheer is a boo

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether cheering was frowned on, then exclaims that the reverse was true.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheers' works twice: as British thanks it gives TA, and as applause its opposite is a jeer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something taboo is socially forbidden, which means it is frowned upon or banned by convention.

clue.text: Henry returning to pay in haste

parts.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

indicators.note: returning is going back the way you came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: taken as written
to foot the bill is to pay it

explanation.surface: A man called Henry coming back to pay up quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversal covers both H and TO, which come out in the order the answer needs.
explanation.definitionFit: Hotfoot is an adverb meaning at speed or in a hurry, as in rushing hotfoot to the scene.

clue.text: Deception lethal, FT ruthlessly demonstrates

indicators.note: to demonstrate is to show, and the phrase shows the answer in its own letters

parts.note: the run starts in the first word and ends inside the last

explanation.surface: A newspaper, the Financial Times, ruthlessly exposes a deadly deception.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs letHAL FT RUTHlessly, using the abbreviation FT whole.
explanation.definitionFit: A half-truth is a statement that is partly true but misleads, a classic form of deception.

clue.text: Sound disapproving note about one franc confection

indicators.note: something about another goes round it, so the outer letters enclose the rest

parts.note: the clicking sound made to show disapproval
the seventh note of the sol-fa scale
the Roman numeral for one
FR is the abbreviation for the French franc

explanation.surface: A disapproving noise about a sweet that costs one franc.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound disapproving' is a noun phrase, the noise itself, not an adjective. The note follows that noise before the pair goes round I and FR, which sit after the second T.
explanation.definitionFit: Tutti-frutti is an ice cream or sweet containing mixed chopped candied fruit, a classic confection.

clue.text: Report of case for Oxonian: E Morse?

indicators.note: a case is the outside of something, so only the outermost letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of the word
in Morse code the letter E is a single short signal, spoken as 'dit'

explanation.surface: A report on a case for an Oxford detective, Endeavour Morse of the TV series.
explanation.walkthrough: Inspector Morse is a fictional Oxford detective whose first name is Endeavour, so 'E Morse' poses as him; really it means the letter E in Morse code. The question mark flags that switch.
explanation.definitionFit: An on dit, borrowed from French 'they say', is a piece of gossip or rumour, an unconfirmed report.

clue.text: Object after husband's made track difficult

indicators.note: 'after X is made Y' describes the state once one thing has been turned into another

parts.note: an object is a thing
H is the abbreviation for husband; this letter is swapped out
RY is the abbreviation for railway, a track; this goes in its place

explanation.surface: Someone complains about what happened after the husband made the course hard.
explanation.walkthrough: Read it as 'object, after husband has been made track': the H in the word for an object becomes RY.
explanation.definitionFit: Trying describes something hard to bear or annoying, so a trying day is a difficult one.

clue.text: Thus overlooked, boy did play, strangely

indicators.note: 'thus' points back at the definition's own manner, so letters in odd positions are passed over and the even ones kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: A boy played in a strange way, and nobody noticed.
explanation.walkthrough: The trick is self-reference: skipping letters 'thus', i.e. oddly, drops the odd-placed ones and keeps the even ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Oddly is an adverb meaning in a peculiar or unusual manner, a near synonym for strangely.

clue.text: Not the clergy's records being recalled in particular

indicators.note: to recall something is to call it back, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: laic means lay, belonging to people who are not clergy
EPs are extended-play records

explanation.surface: Lay people's archives are being reviewed with a particular purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of 'clergy's' belongs to the second piece: the lay person's records, LAIC'S EPS, are then reversed as one string.
explanation.definitionFit: Special and particular are synonyms meaning specific or distinct, as in 'in particular' versus 'in special cases'.

clue.text: Had food finally landed in appropriate place, at long last?

indicators.note: something placed in another is enclosed by it

parts.note: the stomach is the right place for food to land
to have food is to eat, past tense

indicators.note: finally points at the end, so only the closing letter is used

parts.note: the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: Asking whether a meal finally reached its proper destination, after a long wait.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate place' only makes sense for food once you think of where food ends up. The question mark admits the definition is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: Belatedly means later than it should have been, which is close to 'at long last' when something finally arrives.

clue.text: Wide river: manage to cross it in pain

indicators.note: to cross something is to stretch over it, so one piece spans another

parts.note: to fare is to get on, to manage
R is the abbreviation for river
aching means in pain

explanation.surface: A broad river: someone struggles across it while hurting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' refers back to the river, so the verb for managing straddles the river's abbreviation, rather than the river being something to swim.
explanation.definitionFit: Far-reaching describes effects that extend widely, so a far-reaching reform is a wide one in scope.

clue.text: Suffering from cold several times bonfires must be built

indicators.note: building puts materials together in a new structure, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time, and several of them make three
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone chilled to the bone insists that bonfires be built again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Several times' looks like 'often', but it is the abbreviation T, used more than once; three of them are needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Frostbitten describes tissue damaged by freezing, a severe injury from exposure to extreme cold.

clue.text: Bounded around home, healthy, and with energy

indicators.note: one thing around another encloses it

parts.note: fit means healthy
to be home is to be in
E is the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Someone leaped about the house, fit and full of vigour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bounded' looks like the verb for leaping, which suits the energetic surface; it is the adjective meaning limited.
explanation.definitionFit: Finite means having limits or boundaries, so something bounded is finite in extent.

clue.text: Expert's characteristic, confrontational position

definitions.note: a noun phrase; the answer is the phrase describing that position

parts.note: a facet is one aspect or characteristic
the possessive turned round: X's Y is Y of X
an ace is an expert

explanation.surface: A specialist's trademark is taking a combative stance.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive must be unpacked: 'expert's characteristic' becomes 'characteristic of expert', which puts the pieces in answer order.
explanation.definitionFit: Face to face means directly opposite someone, the stance of a confrontation or direct meeting.

clue.text: Both mum and aunt finally, sadly, showing little character

indicators.note: sadly suggests something gone wrong, so the letters are put in a disordered state

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the closing letter is kept

parts.note: the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: Mother and aunt both, in the end, unhappily show little strength of character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little character' looks like a judgement on the women, but it means a tiny fictional figure. 'And' joins the two fodder pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Thumb is the thumb-sized hero of English folklore, the archetypal tiny person in fairy tales.

clue.text: Stony ridge linked to football training

parts.note: a bank is a raised ridge of earth
RU is Rugby Union, a code of football
PT is physical training

explanation.surface: A rocky ridge connected with practice sessions on a football field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stony' looks like rocky, matching the ridge, but it is short for the British slang 'stony broke', meaning penniless.
explanation.definitionFit: Stony, from British slang stony-broke, means having no money at all, as a bankrupt person has.

clue.text: Disturbance over waiter's tip, followed by row

parts.note: time is up when it is over

indicators.note: a tip is an extremity, here the final one, so only the end letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word
to row you pull an oar

explanation.surface: A fuss breaks out over the gratuity left for a waiter, followed by an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip' looks like money left for service but means an end of the word. 'Row' rhymes with cow in the surface, but here it means propelling a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: An uproar is a loud public disturbance or commotion, a noisy outcry.

clue.text: Poor old constable to bat, getting a pair — that was funny!

indicators.note: something poor is in bad shape, so the letters are knocked out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cricket report: a hapless veteran policeman goes in to bat and gets a pair, which raised a laugh.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, 'getting a pair' means being out for nought in both innings, which fits the poor batsman; in the definition it simply means a duo.
explanation.definitionFit: Bud Abbott and Lou Costello were a famous American comedy double act of the 1940s and 1950s.

clue.text: What you see before eruption upset island paradise

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned up, so the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: before a volcano erupts, there is no molten rock to see: 'no lava'

explanation.surface: Seeing an island idyll before a volcano blows and wrecks it.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is answered by a two-word description of a quiet volcano, then turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Avalon is the legendary isle of Arthurian myth where King Arthur was taken, a blessed otherworld.

clue.text: Life's good for flourishing South London area

indicators.note: to flourish is also to wave something about with a flamboyant twirl, so the letters are swung into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
S is the abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: Things are going well for a thriving district in the south of the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'South London area' wants to be read as one place; 'South' is a letter in the fodder and the area is just in London. The Isle of Dogs is the Docklands peninsula in a loop of the Thames.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Dogs is a district of East London on a Thames peninsula, home to Canary Wharf.

clue.text: Stud resembling star affixed to cape

indicators.note: something affixed is attached directly alongside, so the pieces join up

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cape on maps
as means like, resembling
a nova is a star that suddenly brightens

explanation.surface: A star-shaped stud attached to a cloak, as jewellery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stud' looks like a decorative fastener but means a womaniser. The last piece is attached after the cape, though the clue names the cape last.
explanation.definitionFit: Casanova was an 18th-century Venetian famed for his seductions, so his name means a womaniser or ladies' man.

clue.text: Be received by television station's original founder

parts.note: a speech that goes down well is received well
the tube is slang for television

indicators.note: original means first, the one from which others come, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Being welcomed by the man who started a TV channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Founder' looks like the noun for whoever set up the station, but it is the verb meaning to sink or fail.
explanation.definitionFit: To go down the tubes is an informal idiom for failing or collapsing, as a ship or business founders.

clue.text: Old monk's high point joining order

parts.note: a ben is a Scottish mountain peak
an edict is an official order

explanation.surface: The high point of an elderly monk's life is entering a religious order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' looks like a monastic order, matching the monk, but it is a command. Ben is Scottish for mountain, as in Ben Nevis.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Benedict of Nursia was the sixth-century founder of Western monasticism and author of its Rule.

clue.text: Settlements: a single one ultimately that hurt the Poles

indicators.note: just one character, the last, is kept from the following word

parts.note: the final letter of the word
ow is the cry when something hurts
N and S, the north and south poles

explanation.surface: A history note: one particular settlement ended up harming the Polish people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Poles' looks like people from Poland but means the two ends of the earth's axis. 'That hurt' reads as a phrase, yet the words are used separately.
explanation.definitionFit: Towns are communities of houses and people, larger than villages, which are settlements by definition.

clue.text: Musical works tell a story, radical on reflection

parts.note: to tell a story is to fib, to lie

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror shows things the other way round

parts.note: a red is a political radical

explanation.surface: Pieces of music narrate a tale, and a firebrand thinks it over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tell a story' sounds like narrating, matching 'musical works', but it is the polite euphemism for fibbing.
explanation.definitionFit: Lieder are German art songs for voice and piano, like those of Schubert, so they are musical compositions.

clue.text: Titled lord, frightfully musical!

indicators.note: something frightful is a horrid mess, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An aristocrat with a title turns out to be terribly fond of music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frightfully musical' reads as an upper-class 'awfully keen on music', but the adverb is the instruction and the last word stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctor Dolittle is the 1967 film musical, later a stage show, about a vet who talks to animals.

clue.text: Old firm keeping tax returns in book

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside

parts.note: Co is the abbreviation for company, a firm

indicators.note: something that returns comes back, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: VAT is value added tax

explanation.surface: An old company keeping its tax returns filed in a ledger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tax returns' looks like the annual paperwork, but 'returns' is the reversal instruction for the tax abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: An octavo is a book size made by folding each sheet into eight leaves, and so a book of that format.

clue.text: What's Easter — and Lent — without a taste of eggs!

parts.words: What's Easter — and Lent — without a taste of eggs!
parts.note: surface reading: a lament that the Easter and Lent seasons pass without a single egg

parts.words: What's Easter — and Lent — without a taste of eggs!
parts.note: setter's reading: Easter's date shifts each year; drop the first letter of 'eggs', an E, from its description and you get the shifting fast that is Lent

explanation.surface: An exclamation about going through Easter and Lent with no chocolate egg to taste.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer describes Easter directly; removing one E from its second word turns FEAST into FAST, which describes Lent. 'A taste of' means just the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Easter is a church festival whose date changes each year with the lunar calendar, the textbook example of a movable feast.

clue.text: Shopkeeper with quiet way of working getting in touch

indicators.note: to get in somewhere is to go inside it

parts.note: to finger something is to touch it
sh is the call for quiet
MO is modus operandi, Latin for a way of working

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper with a discreet manner contacts people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting in touch' reads as making contact, but 'touch' is a verb meaning to handle, and the first two pieces go inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A fishmonger is a retailer who sells fish from a shop or stall, a particular kind of shopkeeper.

clue.text: Millions, unhealthy and lean, are those up for spam?

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for million
ailing means unwell
a ship that leans to one side lists
surface padding joining the last two pieces

explanation.surface: Asks whether millions of sick, thin people are the ones who would eat tinned meat.
explanation.walkthrough: Spam is a tinned luncheon meat, which suits the hungry surface; the definition means junk email. 'Those up for' means the people targeted.
explanation.definitionFit: A mailing list is the roster of addresses that receive bulk messages, the usual targets of spam email.

clue.text: Old dictator seeing money accrued after election is endless

indicators.note: without an end, so the final letter is dropped
coming after something means standing behind it, so the first-named piece is placed second

parts.note: a poll is an election, minus its last letter
a pot is money built up, as in a jackpot

explanation.surface: A former tyrant sees the money building up after voting day, and there is no end to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' sets the money behind the shortened election, so the order is the reverse of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Pol Pot led the Khmer Rouge regime that ruled Cambodia brutally from 1975 to 1979.

clue.text: Kid is very loud after tea

indicators.note: coming after something means standing behind it, so the first-named piece is placed second

parts.note: cha is British slang for tea
ff, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud

explanation.surface: A child is extremely noisy once teatime is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kid' looks like a noun for a child but is the verb to tease. Cha (or char) is old British slang for tea.
explanation.definitionFit: To chaff someone is to tease or banter with them good-naturedly, which is what kidding someone means.

clue.text: Red oligarch's broadcast one offering a mouthpiece for Havana?

definitions.text: one offering a mouthpiece for Havana?

indicators.note: broadcasting scatters something widely, like seed, so the letters are flung apart

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A communist magnate's radio broadcast acts as a voice for the Cuban government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A mouthpiece for Havana' looks like a spokesman for Cuba's capital, but a Havana is a cigar and the mouthpiece is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: A cigar holder is a tube in which a cigar sits so it can be smoked through its end, a mouthpiece for one.

clue.text: Promoter with loudspeaker outside party, back to get under one's skin

definitions.note: a verb phrase; the answer names the instrument that does it

indicators.note: one thing outside another encloses it

parts.note: a hyper is a publicist, someone who hypes things

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the letters run in reverse

parts.note: a do is a party
a mic, or microphone, amplifies a speaker's voice

explanation.surface: A publicist with a megaphone outside a party, returning to irritate people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get under one's skin' means annoy in the surface, but the definition is literal: a needle that goes beneath the skin.
explanation.definitionFit: A hypodermic is a syringe whose needle injects drugs beneath the skin, so it literally gets under it.

clue.text: Nonsense about basic fitness of course good reason for scepticism

indicators.note: one thing about another goes round it

parts.note: crap is vulgar slang for nonsense
a meal course's most basic quality is being fit to eat
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Dismissing as rubbish the claims about basic fitness on a training course gives good grounds for doubt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' looks like 'naturally', but 'course' is a dish in a meal, and fitness means being fit to eat.
explanation.definitionFit: A credibility gap is the distance between what is claimed and what is believed, a cause for doubt about statements.

clue.text: Ann with shires working thus?

indicators.note: something worked is shaped and kneaded, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
joins the two parts of the fodder

explanation.surface: A woman named Ann working her shire horses: is this how they are equipped?
explanation.walkthrough: Shires are big draught horses, so a farmer working them would have them harnessed; the whole clue describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In harness describes horses fitted with straps for pulling, and figuratively anyone at work in their job.

clue.text: For physicist, a very disastrous error having a doctor round

parts.note: taken as written
V is the abbreviation for very
an own goal, OG, is a calamitous blunder in football
a, plus DR for doctor
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A scientist made a terrible mistake by getting a medic to visit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' looks like 'around', suggesting a container, but it just supplies a ring-shaped letter at the end. An own goal is a football player putting the ball in their own net.
explanation.definitionFit: Amedeo Avogadro was an Italian scientist whose law and constant underpin physics and chemistry.

clue.text: US president collected papers for one from the South

parts.note: a collected person is calm, cool
ID papers are identity documents

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming from the south means reading upwards, bottom to top

parts.note: eg, for example, means for one

explanation.surface: An American president gathered documents, one example coming from the Southern states.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collected' looks like gathered, matching papers, but it means composed. 'The South' suggests the US region; here it is the bottom of the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Calvin Coolidge was the 30th President of the United States, serving from 1923 to 1929.

clue.text: One going left hot drink close to pram: naughty!

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: in an across answer, travelling leftwards means reading from right to left

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps
to drink a little is to sip

indicators.note: the close of something is its end, so only the last letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A child left a hot drink next to the pushchair, which was a mischievous thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going left' sounds like departing, but it reverses everything after it, not the opening numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Impish means mischievous like a little imp, which is how a cheekily naughty child behaves.

clue.text: Shrink understood Leo — only for so long

indicators.note: to shrink something is to make it smaller, so the outer parts are trimmed and a stretch inside survives

parts.note: the run starts inside the first word and ends on the first letter of the last

explanation.surface: A psychiatrist grasped that a Leo was going to be in his life only briefly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shrink' looks like a noun for a psychiatrist, the one who understood Leo, but it is the verb. The answer runs underSTOOD LEO Only.
explanation.definitionFit: Toodle-oo is a jaunty old British way of saying goodbye, and so long is another informal farewell.

clue.text: What bishops may grasp about different men

parts.note: c, for circa, means about
rooks are chessmen other than the bishops just mentioned

explanation.surface: What churchmen might clutch concerning assorted men, perhaps criminals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Men' means chess pieces, and the different ones are the castles rather than the bishops; 'about' is the Latin abbreviation c., circa.
explanation.definitionFit: A bishop's crook, or crozier, is the hooked staff carried as a symbol of the shepherd's role.

clue.text: University fellow stretched, evidently, to a higher level

parts.note: U is the abbreviation for university
Phil is a man's name, and stretching it makes it one letter longer by doubling its final L

explanation.surface: A college don plainly pushed himself to reach a higher standard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Evidently' signals that the stretching is visible in the spelling: the name gains an extra letter. 'Fellow' looks like a college fellow, but it is just any man.
explanation.definitionFit: Uphill means going up a slope, moving towards higher ground, so it travels to a higher level.

clue.text: Old-fashioned daughter walked on over

parts.note: retro means imitating an older style
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A traditional daughter stepped over something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' looks like a reversal signal for a down clue, but it belongs to the definition: walked on over again.
explanation.definitionFit: Retrod is the past tense of retread, to tread again, so it means walked on once more.
